bibliographic.title: Beyond action valuation: A deep reinforcement learning framework for optimizing player decisions in soccer

scope.rationale: Proposes a deep RL framework that goes beyond action valuation by deriving optimal team policies for ball-destination decisions, using tracking + event data modelled as a Markov Decision Process with policy-gradient optimisation.

model.name: Expected Possession Outcome (EPO) optimisation framework
inputs: (x,y) locations of all 22 players and the ball at 25 Hz
x and y velocity components of attacking and defending players
Euclidean distance of the ball to each pitch location
Euclidean distance of the defending team goal to each pitch location
angle between the ball and the goal for each pitch location
cosine of the angle between the ball and the goal for each pitch location
sine of the angle between the ball and the goal for each pitch location
11 input channels of size 105x68 representing the pitch
model.target: Selection probability surface (softmax over 105x68=7140 pitch zones for ball destination) and success probability surface (sigmoid per zone for possession retention); optimised via policy gradient to maximise Expected Possession Outcome (EPO) in (-1, +1)
model.architecture: Encoder-decoder convolutional policy network over 11 x 105 x 68 pitch channels with two output heads (softmax selection surface, sigmoid success surface) and a reconstruction decoder; off-policy policy-gradient fine-tuning
model.spatial_resolution: 105x68 pitch grid (7140 disjoint 1x1 m zones); continuous action space also used
model.temporal_horizon: until end of possession (discounted with gamma=0.99)

metrics: improvement in expected goal difference per game
evaluation.splits: Chronological 80%-10%-10% train/validation/test split respecting game order

claims.statement: The proposed policy network achieves a log-loss of 0.18 with inference time 7.78 seconds (431,354 parameters) for the selection surface, beating logistic regression (0.68 log-loss, 151s) and XGBoost (0.65 log-loss, 127s) on all passes in the test set.

For the success surface, the proposed network achieves log-loss 0.22 with inference time 2.27 seconds (331,276 parameters), beating Naive (0.45), logistic regression (0.57, 372s) and XGBoost (0.58, 351s).

In a league-wide model, behavioural policy EPO is focused around -0.01 (likely to lose a possession by 1% chance), while following the optimal policy yields EPO focused around 0.015 according to importance sampling (1.5% chance of scoring), an improvement of +2.5 expected goals per game over 100 possessions.
Club Brugge's behavioural mean EPO is 0.0046 versus optimal mean EPO 0.0215, an EPO difference of 0.016 corresponding to +1.6 improvement in expected goal difference per game.
Beerschot has the largest team-level EPO difference of 0.032 (+3.2 expected goal difference per game improvement) when switching from behavioural to optimal policy.

Optimal policy proposes a larger propensity of backward passes on the wings (+63% left wing, +87% right wing), a smaller propensity of backward passes in the half-spaces (-53% left half-space, -41% right half-space), and a larger propensity of forward passes (+33%) and sideway passes (+50%) in the centre.

Teams at the top of the table (e.g., Union SG) show small EPO improvements (0.005, +0.5 goals) because their behavioural policy is nearly the same as the optimal policy, while teams at the bottom of the table show larger improvements.
The discount factor gamma is set to 0.99 after tuning with the discount trap method.

The dataset consists of all 330 games of the 2020-21 season and 100 games of 2021-22 of the Belgian Pro League collected by Stats Perform up to October 2021; tracking is sampled at 25 observations per second.

The authors evaluate the optimal policy with three off-policy evaluation methods: importance sampling, doubly robust, and reconstructed possessions (Sim), all of which show similar improvements over the behavioural policy.

limitations: The assumed +2.5 expected goal-difference improvement per game in the league-wide model is not realistic in the real world, as it assumes all players can perfectly follow the optimal policy.
Online experiments to validate the optimal policy in a real match are infeasible; evaluation must rely on off-policy methods.
Hand-crafted features such as team tactics and formations can decrease log-loss further but have long inference time that makes them impractical for the analysis.
Authors could not construct a Naive baseline for the selection surface, only for the success surface.
The choice of negative reward for unsuccessful actions (negative xG for the opponent) is described as an arbitrary choice.
open_questions: Expand the current framework to capture the contributions of individual players so they could adapt themselves to their team-specific optimal strategy.
